title: Applied Economics
text:
Course description
This is the website of the course Applied Economics at the University of Vienna, Winter 2026/2027.
Content updated weekly.
In this course, students reinforce the tools learned in Introductory Econometrics (BA) by applying them to real-world datasets using econometric software. Prior knowledge at that level is assumed throughout. The aim is for students to gain hands-on experience analyzing observational data with the open-source programming language R, and to acquire the tools to carry out empirical research projects independently.

title: 1  Introduction to R
text:
1.2 R Objects

1.2.1 Scalar objects

# Create object "n"
n <- 100

# Print the object in the console:
n

[1] 100




1.2.2 Functions
A function takes one or more objects as input, performs a task, and returns an output. We have already used several, such as sample(), length() and data.frame(). We can also write our own:

ls()

[1] "n"



# Define the function "square()"
square <- function(x) { return(x^2) }

# Run function on object, store as "result"
result <- square(n)

# Print the result in the console
print(result)

[1] 10000



ls()

[1] "n"      "result" "square"




1.2.3 Vectors

# generate vector "age":
age <- sample(18:65, n, replace = TRUE)


# Visualize
age # Print object in console

AirPassengers is a dataset that comes built into R: the monthly totals of international airline passengers, in thousands, from January 1949 to December 1960. Stores information in three vectors:

# Three vectors with one value per month
passengers <- as.numeric(AirPassengers)
year       <- as.numeric(floor(time(AirPassengers)))
month      <- as.numeric(cycle(AirPassengers))

length(passengers)     # 144

[1] 144



# Access elements of a vector
passengers[1]          # first element: 112

[1] 112

passengers[1:3]        # elements 1 to 3: 112 118 132

[1] 112 118 132

passengers[c(1, 144)]  # first and last: 112 432

[1] 112 432




1.2.4 Dataframes
A dataframe is a two-dimensional object that stores data as a table, with rows and columns:

Each row is one observation (an individual, a month, a country, …).
Each column is one variable (income, education, number of passengers, …).










Every column of a dataframe is a vector, and all columns have the same length. So if we have several vectors of the same length, where position 1 in each vector refers to the same observation, position 2 to the next one, and so on, we can put them side by side as the columns of a dataframe with data.frame(). The three vectors year, month and passengers each have 144 elements, one per month, so together they form a dataframe with 144 rows and 3 columns:

# Create a dataset from the three vectors
df_air <- data.frame(year, month, passengers)
dim(df_air)            # 144 rows, 3 columns

[1] 144   3



head(df_air)

  year month passengers
1 1949     1        112
2 1949     2        118
3 1949     3        132
4 1949     4        129
5 1949     5        121
6 1949     6        135

title: 1  Introduction to R
text:
1.3 R Packages
A package is a collection of functions, data and documentation written by other R users, which extends what R can do. R comes with a basic set of functions (such as mean() or data.frame()), and packages add new ones for specific tasks. For example, dplyr adds functions to manipulate dataframes and ggplot2 adds functions to draw graphs. Thousands of packages are freely available on CRAN, the official R package repository.
Using a package takes two steps. First, install it, which downloads it to your computer. This is done only once per computer:
# Install once (downloads from CRAN)
install.packages("dplyr")
Second, load it with library(), which makes its functions available in your current R session. This has to be done every time you start R, so the library() lines usually go at the top of the script:

# Load every time you start R
library(dplyr)

title: 2  Datasets in R
text:
2.1 Inspecting Dataframes
Before running any analysis, take a first look at the data: how large it is, which variables it contains, what values they take, and whether anything is missing. This helps to spot mistakes early, for example a merge that dropped observations or a variable stored in the wrong units.
We use df_air, the monthly passenger dataset created in Chapter 1, as an example.

text:

title: 2  Datasets in R
text:
2.3 Creating Variables

2.3.1 From existing variables
A new variable is created by assigning a vector to a name that does not yet exist in the dataframe, with dataframe$new_variable <- .... The vector is usually computed from existing variables. passengers is measured in thousands, so dividing it by 1000 gives the number of passengers in millions:

df_air$passengers_millions <- df_air$passengers / 1000
head(df_air)

  year month passengers passengers_millions
1 1949     1        112               0.112
2 1949     2        118               0.118
3 1949     3        132               0.132
4 1949     4        129               0.129
5 1949     5        121               0.121
6 1949     6        135               0.135




2.3.2 Logical conditions
A logical condition compares values and returns TRUE or FALSE for each element of a vector. The most common operators are:



Operator
Meaning




==
equal to


!=
not equal to


>, >=
greater than, greater than or equal to


<, <=
less than, less than or equal to


&
and: both conditions are true


\|
or: at least one condition is true


%in%
the value is one of a set of values



The following condition is TRUE for the months between 1950 and 1959. table() counts how many observations satisfy it:

# Logical condition vector
index_fifties <- (df_air$year >= 1950) & (df_air$year <= 1959)
table(index_fifties)

index_fifties
FALSE  TRUE 
   24   120 




2.3.3 Variables based on a condition
ifelse() returns one value where a condition is TRUE and another where it is FALSE, which makes it useful for creating categorical variables. We create two categorical variables: season separates the summer months from the rest of the year, and traffic separates the months with more passengers than the median month from the others:

df_air$season  <- ifelse(df_air$month %in% 6:8, "Summer", "Rest of year")
df_air$traffic <- ifelse(df_air$passengers > median(df_air$passengers), "High", "Low")

table(df_air$season)


Rest of year       Summer 
         108           36 




2.3.4 Two-way tables
With two variables, table() returns a two-way table (or cross-table), which counts the observations for each combination of categories:

table(df_air$season, df_air$traffic)

              
               High Low
  Rest of year   51  57
  Summer         21  15


prop.table() turns the counts into shares. With margin = 1, the shares add up to one within each row:

prop.table(table(df_air$season, df_air$traffic), margin = 1)

              
                    High       Low
  Rest of year 0.4722222 0.5277778
  Summer       0.5833333 0.4166667




2.3.5 Selecting observations with a condition
Generate a new dataset df_air_fifties by selecting the observations/rows that match the condition in index_fifties:

df_air_fifties <- df_air[index_fifties, ]
dim(df_air_fifties)

[1] 120   6




2.3.6 Creating variables with dplyr
The old-fashioned way creates one variable at a time, repeating the name of the dataframe each time:
df_air$passengers_millions <- df_air$passengers / 1000
The dplyr way starts from the dataframe and passes it to mutate() with the pipe |>. Inside mutate(), variables are referred to by their name alone, and several new variables can be created at once. lag() returns the value of the previous row, so lag(passengers) is the number of passengers in the previous month and lag(passengers, 12) the number in the same month of the previous year:

df_air <- df_air |>
  mutate(passengers_millions = passengers / 1000,
         growth_monthly      = (passengers - lag(passengers)) / lag(passengers),
         growth_yearly       = (passengers - lag(passengers, 12)) / lag(passengers, 12))

The first month has no previous month, and the first 12 months have no previous year, so the growth rates are missing (NA) in those rows:

head(df_air[, c("year", "month", "passengers", "passengers_millions", "growth_monthly", "growth_yearly")], 14)

title: 2  Datasets in R
text:
2.4 Multiple Datasets
In this section we work with a second dataset, longley, and later combine it with df_air.

2.4.1 A second dataset: longley
longley is a dataset that comes built into R, with yearly macroeconomic data for the United States from 1947 to 1962. Each row is one year, and each column is one of the following seven variables:








Variable
Description
Units




GNP.deflator
GNP implicit price deflator, a measure of the price level
index, 1954 = 100


GNP
Gross National Product
billions of current US dollars


Unemployed
number of unemployed people
tens of thousands of people


Armed.Forces
number of people in the armed forces
tens of thousands of people


Population
non-institutionalized population aged 14 or older
millions of people


Year
the year of the observation
calendar year


Employed
number of employed people
millions of people



For example, in 1947 the value of Unemployed is 235.6, which means about 2.36 million unemployed people, and the value of Employed is 60.323, which means about 60.3 million employed people.

# longley: US macroeconomic data, one row per year (1947-1962)
data(longley)
class(longley)

[1] "data.frame"


longley data features 7 variables, 16 observations:

dim(longley)

[1] 16  7

head(longley)

     GNP.deflator     GNP Unemployed Armed.Forces Population Year Employed
1947         83.0 234.289      235.6        159.0    107.608 1947   60.323
1948         88.5 259.426      232.5        145.6    108.632 1948   61.122
1949         88.2 258.054      368.2        161.6    109.773 1949   60.171
1950         89.5 284.599      335.1        165.0    110.929 1950   61.187
1951         96.2 328.975      209.9        309.9    112.075 1951   63.221
1952         98.1 346.999      193.2        359.4    113.270 1952   63.639




2.4.2 Aggregating data
Suppose we now want to combine the information in df_air with the information in longley. There is a problem: df_air is a monthly dataset, while longley is annual. Before we can combine them, both datasets need to have the same frequency, so we first aggregate df_air from monthly to annual data.

head(df_air)

  year month passengers passengers_millions       season traffic growth_monthly
1 1949     1        112               0.112 Rest of year     Low             NA
2 1949     2        118               0.118 Rest of year     Low     0.05357143
3 1949     3        132               0.132 Rest of year     Low     0.11864407
4 1949     4        129               0.129 Rest of year     Low    -0.02272727
5 1949     5        121               0.121 Rest of year     Low    -0.06201550
6 1949     6        135               0.135       Summer     Low     0.11570248
  growth_yearly
1            NA
2            NA
3            NA
4            NA
5            NA
6            NA



# Aggregate the monthly data to one row per year
df_air_annual <- df_air |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(annual_passengers       = sum(passengers),
            mean_monthly_passengers = mean(passengers),
            min_monthly_passengers  = min(passengers),
            max_monthly_passengers  = max(passengers))

head(df_air_annual)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
   year annual_passengers mean_monthly_passengers min_monthly_passengers
  <dbl>             <dbl>                   <dbl>                  <dbl>
1  1949              1520                    127.                    104
2  1950              1676                    140.                    114
3  1951              2042                    170.                    145
4  1952              2364                    197                     171
5  1953              2700                    225                     180
6  1954              2867                    239.                    188
# ℹ 1 more variable: max_monthly_passengers <dbl>




2.4.3 Merging datasets
After aggregating the data to the “highest” common denominator, we want to combine the two datasets in a single dataset.
Merging (or joining) two datasets means putting their columns side by side, matching the rows that refer to the same observation. The variable used to match the rows is called the key. Here the key is the year, which is called year in df_air_annual and Year in longley, so we tell dplyr that they are the same variable with by = c("year" = "Year").
New problem: The two datasets do not cover the same years: df_air_annual covers 1949 to 1960 (12 years), while longley covers 1947 to 1962 (16 years).

df_air_annual$year

 [1] 1949 1950 1951 1952 1953 1954 1955 1956 1957 1958 1959 1960

longley$Year

 [1] 1947 1948 1949 1950 1951 1952 1953 1954 1955 1956 1957 1958 1959 1960 1961
[16] 1962


dplyr has several join functions, which differ only in what they do with the rows that have no match in the other dataset. In x |> some_join(y), x is the left dataset and y is the right dataset:








Function
Rows it keeps
Rows in our example




inner_join()
only the rows with a match in both datasets
12 (1949 to 1960)


left_join()
all rows of the left dataset
12 (1949 to 1960)


right_join()
all rows of the right dataset
16 (1947 to 1962)


full_join()
all rows of both datasets
16 (1947 to 1962)



inner_join() keeps only the years that appear in both datasets:

# Merge the two annual datasets, keeping the years present in both
df_inner <- df_air_annual |>
  inner_join(longley, by = c("year" = "Year"))

dim(df_inner)

[1] 12 11

head(df_inner)

# A tibble: 6 × 11
   year annual_passengers mean_monthly_passengers min_monthly_passengers
  <dbl>             <dbl>                   <dbl>                  <dbl>
1  1949              1520                    127.                    104
2  1950              1676                    140.                    114
3  1951              2042                    170.                    145
4  1952              2364                    197                     171
5  1953              2700                    225                     180
6  1954              2867                    239.                    188
# ℹ 7 more variables: max_monthly_passengers <dbl>, GNP.deflator <dbl>,
#   GNP <dbl>, Unemployed <dbl>, Armed.Forces <dbl>, Population <dbl>,
#   Employed <dbl>


left_join() keeps every row of the left dataset, df_air_annual, and adds the longley variables to it. Since every year in df_air_annual also appears in longley, the result has the same 12 rows as with inner_join():

df_left <- df_air_annual |>
  left_join(longley, by = c("year" = "Year"))

dim(df_left)

[1] 12 11


right_join() keeps every row of the right dataset, longley, so the result has 16 rows. The years 1947, 1948, 1961 and 1962 have no match in df_air_annual, so the passenger variables are missing (NA) in those rows:

df_right <- df_air_annual |>
  right_join(longley, by = c("year" = "Year"))

dim(df_right)

[1] 16 11

# Rows without passenger data
df_right[is.na(df_right$annual_passengers), c("year", "annual_passengers", "GNP")]

# A tibble: 4 × 3
   year annual_passengers   GNP
  <dbl>             <dbl> <dbl>
1  1947                NA  234.
2  1948                NA  259.
3  1961                NA  518.
4  1962                NA  555.


Which join to use depends on which observations you want to keep. A left join is the most common choice: it keeps your main dataset intact and adds information from a second one, without dropping or adding rows.


2.4.4 Missing values
is.na() returns TRUE for every missing value. Since R counts TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0, sum() gives the number of missing values in a variable, and colSums() gives it for every variable of a dataframe:

sum(is.na(df_right$annual_passengers))

[1] 4

colSums(is.na(df_right))

                   year       annual_passengers mean_monthly_passengers 
                      0                       4                       4 
 min_monthly_passengers  max_monthly_passengers            GNP.deflator 
                      4                       4                       0 
                    GNP              Unemployed            Armed.Forces 
                      0                       0                       0 
             Population                Employed 
                      0                       0 


Many functions return NA if the variable contains missing values. Adding na.rm = TRUE tells them to ignore the missing values:

mean(df_right$annual_passengers)

[1] NA

mean(df_right$annual_passengers, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 3363.583

title: 3  Scraping Data
text:
3.1 Introduction
In applied economics research, the data needed to answer a question is rarely available in a single dataset: it is usually scattered across multiple sources. In Chapter 2, we enriched a main dataset by merging it with a second, ready-made dataset. Often, however, the additional information we need is not available as a dataset at all, but only as web content. In this session, we learn how to collect such information from the web, store it in a dataframe, and merge it with our main dataset.

title: 3  Scraping Data
text:
3.1.1 Direct Download
Many websites offer a direct download of their data in a ready-to-use format, such as CSV or Excel. For example, the Bureau of Transportation Statistics offers a direct download of the flights dataset we used in Chapter 2. In that case, we can simply download the file and read it into R with read.csv() or read_excel(). However, many websites do not offer a direct download, and we have to collect the information from their web pages.


3.1.2 API-s
Some websites offer an API (Application Programming Interface): a service designed for researchers to request data directly. We request the data by visiting a specific web address that describes what we want, and the API answers in a structured format, typically JSON, which R can convert into lists and dataframes.
For example, the OpenWeather API provides current, forecast and historical weather data for any location in the world. The address https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=New%20York&units=metric&appid=YOUR_KEY asks for the current weather in New York, in metric units, and the answer contains the temperature, humidity, wind speed and cloud cover, with no layout or formatting to remove. The last part of the address, appid, is a personal key: like many APIs, OpenWeather asks users to register (for free) to obtain a key, which identifies who is requesting the data and limits how many requests each user can make.
When a website offers an API, it is usually the better option: the data is cleaner, the format does not change when the website is redesigned, and the website controls how much data can be requested. Many data providers relevant for economists, such as the World Bank, Eurostat or the FRED database of the Federal Reserve, offer APIs. Scraping is the fallback for information that is only available on web pages.


3.1.3 Webscrapping
A lot of useful information is available on websites but not as a downloadable or API-accessible dataset: it is displayed on web pages, written for people to read rather than for computers to analyse. Web scraping means writing code that visits these pages automatically, extracts the pieces of information we need, and stores them in a dataframe. A web page is written in HTML, a language that marks every part of the page (a title, a table, a row of a table) with a tag. A scraper reads the HTML of a page and uses these tags to find the information it is looking for, such as the value in the row labelled “Elevation” of a table.

title: 3  Scraping Data
text:
3.2 Webscrapping in R
Web scraping code can be written in many programming languages. Python is probably the most popular choice, with packages such as requests, BeautifulSoup and Selenium, and many online tutorials and examples are written in Python. The steps are the same in every language, though: request a page, read its HTML, extract the information, and store it in a dataset. In this course we stick to R, so that we can collect, clean, merge and analyse the data with the same tools we use for the rest of the course.

3.2.1 Packages
In R, web scraping relies mainly on three packages:








Package
What it does
Example functions




rvest
reads the HTML of a web page and extracts its parts, such as tables, rows or text
read_html() reads a page; html_element() and html_elements() select its parts; html_text2() extracts their text; html_table() turns an HTML table into a dataframe


stringr
cleans the extracted text, for example to keep only the number in “312 ft (95 m)”
str_extract() keeps the part of a text that matches a pattern; str_remove_all() deletes parts of a text; str_detect() checks whether a text contains a pattern


httr
sends requests to websites and to their APIs (services that return data directly, rather than a page to display)
GET() sends a request to a web address; status_code() checks whether it succeeded; content() extracts the answer



Like dplyr, they are installed once with install.packages() and loaded with library() every time we use them:
library(rvest)
library(httr)
library(stringr)
Writing a scraper used to be a tedious process, often requiring extensive programming skills: we had to study the HTML of the pages, find the tags that contain the information, and handle the many pages that do not follow the expected format. Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT or Claude have made this much easier. We can describe in plain words what we want the code to do and let the LLM write it, an approach known as vibecoding. Vibecoding does not make our own understanding unnecessary, though: the code an LLM writes often runs without errors but returns incomplete or wrong information. We still need to read the code, check its output, and ask for corrections, as we will do in this session.
When scraping, keep in mind that each request uses the resources of the website. Scrapers should pause between requests and respect the website’s terms of use.


3.2.2 Base Dataset flights
Package nycflights13 includes the The flights dataset, which contains information on all 336.776 flights departing from New York City airports (JFK, LGA, EWR) in 2013. The dataset contains the following 19 variables:

year, month, day: date of departure.
dep_time, arr_time: actual departure and arrival times, in local time, written as HHMM (e.g. 517 means 5:17).
sched_dep_time, sched_arr_time: scheduled departure and arrival times, in the same format.
dep_delay, arr_delay: departure and arrival delays, in minutes. Negative values mean the flight departed or arrived early.
carrier: two-letter code of the airline (e.g. UA for United Airlines).
flight: flight number.
tailnum: tail number, which identifies the plane.
origin, dest: three-letter codes of the airports of origin and destination.
air_time: time spent in the air, in minutes.
distance: distance between the two airports, in miles.
hour, minute: scheduled departure time, split into hours and minutes.
time_hour: scheduled date and hour of departure, stored as a date-time variable.

3.2.3 Complementary Dataset: airports
We want to study how airport features determine flight delays. To do this, we need to enrich the flights dataset with additional information about each airport features, such as its location, altitude, and runway information. The nycflights13 package contains a complementary dataset called airports, which contains some of this information for all airports in the United States. It has 1,458 rows (one per airport) and the following 8 variables:

faa: three-letter FAA code of the airport (e.g. JFK). It matches the origin and dest variables of flights, so it is the key for merging the two datasets.
name: name of the airport.
lat, lon: latitude and longitude of the airport, in decimal degrees. Longitudes west of Greenwich are negative, so all US airports have a negative longitude.
alt: altitude above sea level, in feet.
tz: time zone, as the difference from GMT in hours (e.g. −5 for New York).
dst: daylight saving time rule: A for the standard US rule, N for no daylight saving time (e.g. Hawaii), U for unknown.
tzone: name of the time zone (e.g. "America/New_York").

We want to further enrich the airports dataset with additional information about each airport infrastructure, such as its number of runways and their longitude. To do this, we will create an a webscraping script to extract this information from each airport’s wikipedia page. For example, the pictures below show the information box of the Wikipedia page of Washington Dulles International Airport.

title: 3  Scraping Data
text:
3.3 Vibecoding a Scrapper
Generate a prompt to your LLM of choice, asking to create a webscraper that extracts the following information from each airport’s Wikipedia page:

3.3.1 First Attempt

# Keep only the airports that appear in flights, as origin or destination
airports <- airports[airports$faa %in% c(flights$origin, flights$dest), ]
nrow(airports)

[1] 103

head(airports$faa)

[1] "ABQ" "ACK" "ALB" "ANC" "ATL" "AUS"


I am working on R. I have a list of unique airport codes from the flights dataset airports$faa. with elements of the list that look as follows: “ABQ” “ACK” “ALB” “ANC” “ATL” “AUS”… I want to extract information about each airport from its Wikipedia page. Write an R script that loops through the list, scrapes the Wikipedia pages (e.g., https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ + airport code), extracts: 1) the number of runways in the airport, 2) the length of each runway, in metres, from the Wikipedia infobox.
A minimal version of the resulting scraper uses the rvest package, which reads a web page and extracts its parts. It is far from perfect: airports whose page is not found are skipped, and airports whose page has no runway table get 0 runways. Since the number of runways differs across airports, the lengths are stored as a single text, separated by semicolons:

library(rvest)

# Empty dataframe to store the results, one row per airport
df_airports_wiki <- data.frame()

for (code in airports$faa) {

  # Read the Wikipedia page of the airport code; skip the code if the page does not exist
  page <- tryCatch(read_html(paste0("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/", code)),
                   error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(page)) next

  # Rows of the runway table, inside the infobox at the top right of the page
  rows <- html_text2(html_elements(page, "table.infobox table tr"))

  # Runway rows start with a runway direction, e.g. "4L/22R  3,353  11,000  Asphalt"
  runways <- strsplit(rows[grepl("^[0-9]+[LCR]?/[0-9]+", rows)], "\t")

  # Lengths in metres: 2nd column, or 3rd if the table lists feet first
  m_col     <- if ("ft\tm" %in% rows) 3 else 2
  lengths_m <- sapply(runways, function(r) r[m_col])

  df_airports_wiki <- rbind(df_airports_wiki, data.frame(
    airport_code    = code,
    n_runways       = length(runways),
    runway_length_m = paste(lengths_m, collapse = "; ")
  ))

  Sys.sleep(0.5) # wait half a second between pages, to be polite to Wikipedia
}

[25] "DAY" "DCA" "DEN" "DFW" "DSM" "GRR" "GSO" "GSP" "HDN" "HNL" "HOU" "IAD"

After that, we can generate a new prompt to the LLM, asking it to improve the scrapper:
The previous scrapper missed the following airports: [paste the list of missed airports here]. Moreover, I want that, if you are unable to find a specific variable, such as no airport runaways n_runways, you record “NA” value instead of 0. If the number of runways is NA, record the runaway length variable runway_length_m as “NA”. Generate a new version of the scrapper.

library(rvest)
library(httr)

# Empty dataframe to store the results, one row per airport
df_airports_wiki2 <- data.frame()

for (code in airports$faa) {

  # New: instead of guessing the page address, ask Wikipedia's search engine
  # for "<code> airport" and take the title of the first result
  search_url <- paste0("https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&list=search",
                       "&format=json&srsearch=", code, "%20airport")
  title <- tryCatch(content(GET(search_url))$query$search[[1]]$title,
                    error = function(e) NULL)

  # Read the Wikipedia page of that title (NULL if the search or the page fails)
  page <- if (is.null(title)) NULL else
    tryCatch(read_html(paste0("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/", URLencode(title))),
             error = function(e) NULL)

  # New: if the page is not found, keep the airport in the dataset with NA values
  if (is.null(page)) {
    df_airports_wiki2 <- rbind(df_airports_wiki2, data.frame(
      airport_code = code, airport_name = NA, n_runways = NA, runway_length_m = NA))
    next
  }

  # Rows of the runway table, inside the infobox at the top right of the page
  rows <- html_text2(html_elements(page, "table.infobox table tr"))

  # Runway rows start with a runway direction, e.g. "4L/22R  3,353  11,000  Asphalt"
  runways <- strsplit(rows[grepl("^[0-9]+[LCR]?/[0-9]+", rows)], "\t")

  # Lengths in metres: 2nd column, or 3rd if the table lists feet first
  m_col     <- if ("ft\tm" %in% rows) 3 else 2
  lengths_m <- sapply(runways, function(r) r[m_col])

  # New: NA instead of 0 if no runways are found, and then also NA for their lengths
  n_runways       <- if (length(runways) == 0) NA else length(runways)
  runway_length_m <- if (is.na(n_runways)) NA else paste(lengths_m, collapse = "; ")

  df_airports_wiki2 <- rbind(df_airports_wiki2, data.frame(
    airport_code    = code,
    airport_name    = title,
    n_runways       = n_runways,
    runway_length_m = runway_length_m
  ))

  Sys.sleep(1) # wait one second between pages, to be polite to Wikipedia
}

title: 3  Scraping Data
text:
3.4 Final Dataset
Remember, df_airports_wiki2 is a complement. We now have to merge it with the base dataset nycflights13 to create a final dataset that contains all the information we need for our analysis.
Each flight involves two airports, so the information in df_airports_wiki2 has to be merged twice: once for the airport of origin and once for the airport of destination. To tell the two apart in the final dataset, we first select the variables we need and rename them with the prefix origin_. The key variable is renamed origin, as in flights, so that the two datasets can be matched by that name:

library(dplyr)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.5.2



Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

# Airport information, with variable names referring to the airport of origin
df_origin <- df_airports_wiki2 |>
  select(origin                 = airport_code,
         origin_n_runways       = n_runways,
         origin_runway_length_m = runway_length_m)

df_flights <- flights |>
  left_join(df_origin, by = "origin")

A left join keeps every flight, so df_flights has the same number of rows as flights, plus the new variables:

dim(flights)

[1] 336776     19

dim(df_flights)

[1] 336776     21


All flights depart from one of the three New York airports, so the origin variables should only take three different values:

table(df_flights$origin, df_flights$origin_n_runways)

     
           2      3      4
  EWR      0 120835      0
  JFK      0      0 111279
  LGA 104662      0      0


Second step, enrich the dataset with the airport of destination information, following the same steps with the prefix dest_:

# Airport information, with variable names referring to the airport of destination
df_dest <- df_airports_wiki2 |>
  select(dest                 = airport_code,
         dest_n_runways       = n_runways,
         dest_runway_length_m = runway_length_m)

df_flights <- df_flights |>
  left_join(df_dest, by = "dest")

dim(df_flights)

[1] 336776     23

write.csv(df_flights, "data/df_flights_enriched.csv", row.names = FALSE)
